summary: Raskolnikov, a poor former law student in Saint Petersburg, kills an old pawnbroker. He believes that an extraordinary man may cross the moral line for a higher goal, and that the money would free him from poverty. After the deed he is overwhelmed by fever, paranoia and guilt. He circles the detective Porfiry, befriends Sonya, who is driven by poverty into prostitution, and faces the sinister Svidrigailov. Sonya reads him the raising of Lazarus. He confesses and is sent to Siberia, where the epilogue points to a slow renewal.
context: Dostoevsky wrote the book in debt after his brother Mikhail died in 1864. He asked the editor Mikhail Katkov for an advance, and the work began as a story and grew into a novel by late 1865. The Russian Messenger ran it in twelve monthly parts in 1866, and it later appeared as one volume. It is the first great novel of his mature period, after his exile in Siberia. The site carries Constance Garnett's translation, set in the Standard Ebooks edition.

people.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
people.note: Russian novelist born in Moscow in 1821 who spent four years in a Siberian labour camp.

people.name: Rodion Raskolnikov
people.note: A destitute former student who murders a pawnbroker and is tormented by his conscience.

people.name: Sonya Marmeladova
people.note: Daughter of a drunkard, forced into prostitution, who reads Raskolnikov the story of Lazarus.

people.name: Porfiry Petrovich
people.note: The detective investigating the murders, who senses that Raskolnikov is guilty.

people.name: Svidrigailov
people.note: Dunya's ill-intentioned former employer, who takes his own life.

people.name: Razumikhin
people.note: Raskolnikov's old university friend, who sees that he is seriously ill.

people.name: Semyon Marmeladov
people.note: A hopeless drunk whose confession moves Raskolnikov while he is still weighing the murder.

people.name: Mikhail Katkov
people.note: Editor of The Russian Messenger, which published the novel in 1866.

people.name: Constance Garnett
people.note: English translator of nearly all of Dostoevsky's fiction, who published this translation in 1914.

places.name: Saint Petersburg
places.note: The setting, a city of poverty and rationalist ideas.

places.name: Sennaya Square
places.note: Critical scenes in the novel take place on this square.

places.name: Brighton
places.note: Birthplace of the translator Constance Garnett.

timeline.label: Dostoevsky is arrested for belonging to the Petrashevsky Circle.
His brother Mikhail dies and Dostoevsky takes on his debts.
In September he writes to Katkov about a young man in the grip of strange ideas.
The Russian Messenger runs the novel in twelve monthly instalments.
Constance Garnett publishes her translation of the novel.

ideas.title: Extraordinary men and crime
ideas.note: Raskolnikov persuades himself that exceptional people may break the law, a theory the plot refutes.

ideas.title: Conscience as true punishment
ideas.note: The book is less about legal consequences than about the torment of Raskolnikov's own conscience.

ideas.title: Radicalism as a moral danger
ideas.note: Dostoevsky planned to examine the dangers of radical ideology in a letter to Katkov.

ideas.title: Suffering and renewal
ideas.note: Sonya and the story of Lazarus lead toward his confession and a slow regeneration.

passages.quote: On an exceptionally hot evening early in July a young man came out of the garret in which he lodged in S⁠⸺ Place and walked slowly, as though in hesitation, towards K⁠⸺ bridge
passages.why: The famous opening: Raskolnikov leaves his garret.

passages.quote: He unbuttoned his coat and freed the axe from the noose, but did not yet take it out altogether, simply holding it in his right hand under the coat
passages.why: The murder scene, told through his numb hands.

passages.quote: “Sonia! Daughter! Forgive!” he cried, and he tried to hold out his hand to her, but losing his balance, he fell off the sofa, face downwards on the floor

“Yes, that’s what it was! I wanted to become a Napoleon, that is why I killed her.⁠ ⁠… Do you understand now?” “N-no,” Sonia whispered naively and timidly

passages.quote: But that is the beginning of a new story⁠—the story of the gradual renewal of a man, the story of his gradual regeneration, of his passing from one world into another, of his initiation into a new unknown life
